kh:body.kh:document-title: Prudential Regulation Authority—structure, functions and duties
kh:body.kh:mini-summary: The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) forms part of the group of regulatory bodies that was put in place on 1 April 2013 following amendment of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA 2000) by the Financial Services Act 2012 (FSA 2012). This Practice Note outlines the PRA’s structure and considers the role and responsibilities of its governing body, the requirements of the annual report and other key governance requirements. This Practice Note also outlines the PRA’s functions as set out in the FSMA 2000, and the manner in which the PRA discharges its functions.

tr:secmain.core:title: Legislation establishing the PRA
tr:secmain.core:para: Financial Services Act 2012Financial Services and Markets Act 2000The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) forms part of the regulatory structure that the UK government put in place on 1 April 2013. The Financial Services Act (FSA 2012) amended the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA 2000) and established the bodies which replaced the Financial Services Authority (FSA) as the regulator for financial services in the UK.

FSMA 2000, Pt 2A, Ch 2 sets out general information about the PRA including details of its objectives, its obligation to consult with practitioners and HM Treasury's power to conduct reviews of its performance.

tr:secmain.core:title: Structure of the PRA
tr:secmain.core:para: The PRA has been structured in this way as it works closely with the Financial Policy Committee (FPC), a committee of the Bank of England (BoE), on prudential regulation.

The PRA was a separate legal entity, and a subsidiary of the BoE. However, the Bank of England and Financial Services Act 2016, ss 12–16, Sch 2, Pt 2 amended the Bank of England Act 1998 (BEA 1998) and FSMA 2000, ended the subsidiary status of the PRA, and as a result of the implementation of those provisions by the Bank of England and Financial Services Act 2016 (Commencement No. 4 and Saving Provision) Regulations 2017, SI 2017/43, since 1 March 2017, the PRA’s functions have been carried out by the BoE acting through its Prudential Regulation Committee (PRC). The Treasury can make recommendations to the Committee about aspects of the government’s economic policy to which the Committee should have regard when carrying out these activities.
According to BEA 1998, s 30A, the PRC is to consist of:

core:listitem.core:para: the Governor of the BoE,
the Deputy Governor for prudential regulation,
the Deputy Governor for financial stability,
the Deputy Governor for markets and banking,
one member appointed by the Governor of the Bank with the approval of the Chancellor of the Exchequer,
the Chief Executive of the FCA, and
at least six members appointed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer

tr:secmain.core:para: The processes and legal framework of the PRA are intended to enhance the exchange of information between it and other parts the BoE and to ensure a coordinated response to a financial crisis. As part of this, the PRA has implemented a more 'judgment-led' approach to prudential regulation, with discretion underpinning its approach to supervision. For further information about the way in which PRA regulates firms, see Practice Notes: Prudential Regulation Authority—supervisory approach—deposit-takers and Prudential Regulation Authority—supervisory approach—insurers.

tr:secmain.core:title: What are the PRA’s functions?
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, s 2AB(1), outlines that the PRA is to have its functions conferred to it under FSMA 2000, and its functions are outlined in FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB. FSMA 2000 also outlines how the PRA discharges its functions.
Any functions conferred to the PRA under FSMA 2000 also include references to functions conferred to it by or under:

core:listitem.core:para: the Insolvency Act 1986
the Banking Act 2009 (BA 2009)
the Financial Services Act 2012, or
the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 (FSMA 2023)

tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, s 2FAny reference in FSMA 2000 in relation to any function of the PRA, or to the objectives of the PRA is a reference to its general objective but:

core:listitem.core:para: so far as the function is exercisable in relation to the activity of effecting or carrying out contracts of insurance, or PRA-authorised persons carrying on that activity, is a reference to its general objective and its insurance objective

so far as the function is exercisable in relation to an activity to which an objective specified by order by virtue of FSMA 2000, s 2D(2) relates, or PRA-authorised persons carrying on that activity, is a reference to its general objective and the objective specified by the order

tr:secmain.core:para: Like the FCA, the PRA is required to have regard to the eight principles of good regulation when exercising its functions. See Practice Note: Prudential Regulation Authority—objectives and principles for further information on the objectives of the PRA, and specified orders.

tr:secmain.core:title: How does the PRA discharge its functions?
tr:secmain.core:para: The general objective of the PRA is to promote the safety and soundness of PRA-authorised firms. To achieve this, it undertakes the following functions:

core:listitem.core:para: collects information about financial stability
supervises PRA-authorised firms (that is, dual-regulated firms)
formulates and implements its own rules and procedures for PRA-authorised firms and their activities, and
works closely with the BoE Special Resolution Unit on planning for and implementing resolutions of failing banks and formulating policies for the Recovery and Resolution Plans

tr:secmain.core:title: The PRA's annual report and audited accounts
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 19(1)The PRA must report to the Treasury at least once each year on the following:

core:listitem.core:para: the discharge of its functions
the extent to which its statutory objectives have been met and its regulatory principles have been taken into account
the remuneration of the members of the governing body
an account of how the PRA has complied with its general duty to coordinate
the use of the PRA veto under FSMA 2000, s 3I and the use of the PRA veto on with-profits issues under FSMA 2000, s 3J
its cooperation with regulatory bodies outside the UK, and
any other matters specified by the Treasury

tr:secmain.core:para: FS(BR)A 2013, ss 12–15Under FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 19(1A) (as inserted by the sections 5(1) and (2) of the Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act 2013 (FS(BR)A 2013) in the report, the PRA must also report in general terms on:

core:listitem.core:para: the extent to which, in its opinion, ‘ring-fenced bodies’ have complied with the ring-fencing provisions. The ring fencing provisions are contained in FSMA 2000, Pt 9B (inserted by FS(BR)A 2013, s 4) and supplemented by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Ring-Fenced Bodies and Core Activities) Order 2014, SI 2014/1960 and the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Excluded Activities and Prohibitions) Order 2014, SI 2014/2080 (as both are amended by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Ring-fenced Bodies, Core Activities, Excluded Activities and Prohibitions) (Amendment) Order 2025, SI 2025/30) and the Ring-Fenced Bodies section of the PRA Rulebook. For more information about ring-fencing provisions, see Practice Note: UK structural banking reform—ring-fencing
steps taken by ring-fenced bodies in order to comply with the ring-fencing provisions
steps taken by it to enforce the ring-fencing provisions

the extent to which ring-fenced bodies are carrying on the regulated activity of dealing in investments as principal (whether in the United Kingdom or elsewhere) in circumstances where as a result of an order under FSMA 2000, s 142D(2) that activity is not an excluded activity

the extent to which ring-fenced bodies are carrying on activities that would be excluded activities by virtue of an order under FSMA 2000, s 142D(4) but for an exemption or exclusion made by such an order
the extent to which ring-fenced bodies are doing things that they would be prohibited from doing by an order under FSMA 2000, s 142E but for an exemption made by such an order, and

the extent to which ring-fenced bodies appear to it to have acted in accordance with any guidance which it has given to ring-fenced bodies and which relates to the operation of the ring-fencing provisions

tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 19(B)For the purposes of FSMA 2000, para 19(1A), 'ring-fenced bodies' refers only to ring-fenced bodies that are PRA-authorised persons, and 'the ring-fencing provisions' means ring-fencing rules and the duty imposed as a result of FSMA 2000, s142G.

FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 20FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 21In relation to the report, the PRA must also at the same time publish a consultation inviting comments and representations from the public within three months from the date of the reports publication. Following this, within four months of the consultation ending, the PRA must publish a report on the consultation which must include a general account of any representations received from the public.
However, unlike the FCA, the PRA is not required to hold an annual public meeting. This has led to some criticism that the PRA lacks accountability.

FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 22FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 1, para 23The PRA must audit and publish its accounts and the accounts must also be laid before Parliament. The PRA's annual report and accounts can be found on the PRA's website.

tr:secmain.core:title: Complaining about the PRA
tr:secmain.core:para: Under FSA 2012, Pt 6, s 84, the PRA was required to implement a process to deal with any complaints made against it in connection with the exercise of, or failure to exercise, any of their relevant functions. They were also required to appoint an independent person (the investigator), subject to Treasury approval, to be responsible for the conduct of investigations in accordance with the complaints scheme.
The complaints scheme had to be designed so that, as far as reasonably practicable, complaints are investigated quickly, and without favouring the PRA.

FSA 2012, Pt 6FSA 2012, s 85For the purposes of FSMA 2000, s 84, the PRA's relevant functions are its functions conferred by or under FSMA 2000 (other than its legislative functions) and such other functions as the Treasury may by order provide. For further information on the functions of the PRA, see What are the PRA’s functions? below.

FSA 2012, Pt 6FSA 2012, s 85The PRA was required to publish and consult on its proposed complaints scheme, and once the PRA made the proposed complaints scheme they were required to publish an account of the representations received and their response. The PRA must also continue to publish up to date details of the complaints scheme, and notify the Treasury of these publications.

The PRA must ensure that investigators have sufficient means and powers to conduct a full investigation. The investigator is required to provide a report to the PRA at the conclusion of the investigation and also to make such a report public.

FSA 2012, Pt 6FSA 2012, s 87The complaints scheme must give the investigator the power to recommend, if appropriate, that the PRA pay compensation or remedies the matter complained of. The PRA must respond to such requirements and the investigator may require it to publish its response either in full or in part.

The PRA may reasonably consider a complaint to be more appropriately dealt with in a different way, for example by referring the matter to the Upper Tribunal. If the PRA opts to do this it must inform the investigator, although the investigator may decide to proceed with its own investigation in any event.

FSA 2012, Pt 6FSA 2012, s 88Neither the investigator, nor a person appointed to conduct an investigation on the investigator's behalf under section is to be liable in damages for anything done or omitted in the discharge, or purported discharge, of functions in relation to the investigation of a complaint. That is unless the act or omission is shown to be in bad faith, or to prevent an award in damages act or omission on the ground that the act or omission was unlawful as a result of section 6(1) of the Human Rights Act 1998 (HRA 1998, s 6(1)).
More information about the complaints scheme can be found on the PRA's website here.
For further information about complaints against the regulators, see Practice Note: Complaints against UK financial services regulators.

tr:secmain.core:title: PRA exemption from liability in damages
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 4, para 33The PRA, its officers, employees and members cannot be held liable for damages in relation to any action or omission related to the discharge of its functions. Exceptions to this include where the relevant acts or omissions are held to be in bad faith, or to prevent an award in damages act or omission on the ground that the act or omission was unlawful as a result of HRA 1998, s 6(1).

tr:secmain.core:title: PRA policies on penalties and fees
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 3, para 28FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 3, para 29The PRA must implement a policy for the penalties it will impose. This policy must not take into account the costs the PRA incurs in discharging its function and should instead be set up to ensure that amounts raised are used for the benefit of PRA authorised persons. The scheme may, however, specify different provisions for different classes of authorised persons. The scheme must also ensure that those who have become liable to pay a penalty to the PRA in any financial year of the PRA do not receive any benefit under the scheme in the following financial year. Please note that the FSMA 2023 introduced several important updates to the UK’s financial services regulatory framework, and certain of these changes amended the PRA’s enforcement powers. In particular, these enforcement powers arise in connection with:

core:listitem.core:para: the extension of BA 2009, Pt 5 to apply in respect of recognised payment systems (RPS) using digital settlement assets (DSAs) and specified service providers to such RPS, and to apply to a new category of persons, namely DSA service providers (DSA SPs), as well as specified service providers to DSA SPs
the creation of BA 2009, Pt 5A which confers powers on the BoE over entities involved in the wholesale distribution of cash, and
the creation of a regime for the oversight of critical third parties (CTPs)

tr:secmain.core:para: The PRA has published a statement of its approach to enforcement policies and procedure, which can be found on its website, here.

FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, Pt 3, para 31The PRA, like the FCA, has the right to levy fees to meet the costs of carrying out its functions, repaying any borrowing and maintaining adequate reserves. Fees due to the PRA are to be recoverable as debts.

tr:secmain.core:title: PRA's duty to consult and engage with others
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, s 2LThe PRA is required to implement arrangements to consult with PRA-authorised persons or, where appropriate, persons appearing to the PRA to represent the interests of such persons on the extent to which its general policies and practices are consistent with its general duties under sections FSMA 2000, s 2B to s 2H.

FSMA 2000, s 2MIn addition, FSMA 2000 created a system of independent ‘panels’ intended to contribute to the FCA's and PRA’s functions. The PRA’s duty to consult mirrors that of the FCA. Like the FCA, arrangements made under FSMA 2000, s 2L, includes the PRA establishing and maintaining a panel of practitioners—the PRA Practitioner Panel with a non-statutory insurance-subcommittee—and to appoint such persons representing PRA-authorised firms as it considered appropriate.
In addition, as a result of amendments made by FSMA 2023 made the following amendments to FSMA 2000 concerning statutory panels:

core:listitem.core:para: FSMA 2000, s 2MA places the PRA’s insurance sub-committee panel, on an equal footing with other statutory panels

FSMA 2000, s 2NA requires the PRA to publish statements of policy on its process for appointing members to its statutory panels. Prior to publishing its statements, it is required to consult HM Treasury
FSMA 2000, s 2NB requires the PRA to mention in their public consultations information on any pre-engagement with statutory panels

FSMA 2000, s 138JA required the PRA to establish and maintain the PRA Cost Benefit Analysis (CBA) Panel to provide advice in relation to cost benefit analyses for the purposes of providing an ‘enhanced external challenge’ to CBA concerning PRA consultations
FSMA 2000, s 138JB requires the PRA to publish a statement of policy on its approach to CBA

FSMA 2000, s 2LA contains additional requirements relating to the composition of the Practitioner, Insurance and CBA Panels. This provision is supplemented by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 (Panel Remuneration and Reports) Regulations 2023, SI 2023/1273 (the Panel Remuneration and Reports Regulations 2023), which permit the PRA to remunerate members of these Panels and require the PRA CBA Panel to make annual reports to HM Treasury. A person who receives remuneration from the FCA, the PRA, the Payment Systems Regulator, the Bank of England or the Treasury is disqualified under FSMA 2000, s 2LA(1) from being appointed as a member of any of the PRA's statutory panels. However, Regulation 2 of the Panel Remuneration and Reports Regulations 2023 makes limited exceptions to these disqualifications for members of the PRA CBA Panel who receive remuneration for their panel work

tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2023 also amends the BEA 1998 and FSMA 2000 concerning how the PRA engages with HM Treasury and others. For example:

core:listitem.core:para: BEA 1998, s 30B requires HM Treasury to send ‘recommendations letters’ on matters of economic policy at least once in every parliament to the PRA, who must then consider the recommendations when performing its functions and respond annually to such recommendations letters

FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZA, Pt 4, para 28 requires the PRA to notify the Treasury Select Committee when it publishes a consultation, and it must respond to any Select Committee that has responded to a consultation published by it

tr:secmain.core:title: PRA coordination with the FCA
tr:secmain.core:para: As both the PRA and the FCA are able to make rules which apply to the same functions of dual-regulated firms (for example, in relation to systems and controls), there is a risk of overlap and confusion between the rule-making functions of the two regulators. This is particularly problematic as the PRA has the power to develop its own designation criteria to determine which investment firms are within its remit (subject to the fact that the PRA may only designate firms if they satisfy certain conditions as set out in FSMA 2000 (PRA-regulated Activities) Order 2013, SI 2013/556—see the PRA's statement of policy on the designation of investment firms, published in March 2013). This is because legislators considered it complex and inflexible to set out the PRA’s scope too prescriptively in FSMA 2000 itself.

FSMA 2000, s 138J requires the PRA, before making any rules, to consult with the FCA. After doing so, the regulator must publish a draft of the proposed rules in the way appearing to the PRA to be best calculated to bring them to the attention of the public.

In its February 2011 consultation paper: 'A new approach to financial regulation: building a stronger system', HM Treasury suggested that in circumstances where the regulators are in conflict over the authorities’ assessment of the impact of a rule on financial stability, they may approach the Financial Policy Committee (FPC) for a recommendation, although there is no statutory obligation to do so.

Further, the updated memorandum of understanding between the FCA and the BoE (exercising its prudential regulation functions) specifies that the FCA and PRA will consult with each other early on in the policy making process on any issues which may have a material effect on the other's objectives. To achieve this they will also hold quarterly meetings to discuss proposed policies. For further information on the FCA, see UK regulators—financial services—overview and Practice Notes: FCA—corporate governanceand Financial Conduct Authority—functions.

tr:secmain.core:title: PRA coordination with the FPC
tr:secmain.core:para: The PRA and the BoE are both responsible for contributing to the macro-prudential supervision of firms. While the FPC is responsible for formulating macro-prudential policy, frequent and consistent information exchanges and discussions are intended between the FPC and the PRA. Any overlap between the two is to be mitigated by cross membership of each regulator’s governing body.

The PRA provides firm-specific information to the FPC which will form part of its review of the macro-prudential outlook. Similarly, the FPC’s assessment of potential systemic risks forms a part of the PRA’s judgments on institutions, sectors and asset classes. See Practice Note: Financial Policy Committee—essentials for information on the powers of the FPC in this regard.

The FPC provides recommendations and directions to the PRA (and also the FCA) on how it should implement regulation and operate its powers for macro-prudential purposes. The PRA is required to execute FPC recommendations on a 'comply or explain' basis and must report to the FPC on implementation. See Practice Note: UK regulators—financial services—overview for further information.

tr:secmain.core:title: PRA and international coordination
tr:secmain.core:para: Under FSA 2012, s 64, the Treasury (on the one hand), the BoE and the PRA (on the other) must arrange to co-ordinate the discharge of their respective functions so far as they relate to the stability of the UK financial system, and affect the public interest.

HM Treasury, the BoE (when carrying out its functions in relation to financial stability and as a regulator), the FCA and the PRA have also adopted a memorandum of understanding on how each regulator will coordinate its responsibilities at an international level. For further information on European and other international bodies, see overviews: EU regulators—financial services—overview and International bodies—financial services regulation—overview.

PRA's approach to banking supervisionThe Prudential Regulation Authority’s approach to insurance supervisionIn the papers published by the BOE on the PRA’s approach to supervision, the significance of the PRA’s responsibilities in participating in global supervisory colleges is particularly emphasised. To be fully effective, colleges must operate in a manner that enables supervisors to be open and transparent with each other, and to address difficult issues. The PRA states that its seeks to adopt this approach when it runs colleges and expects other authorities to participate on the same basis. See Practice Notes: Prudential Regulation Authority—supervisory approach—deposit-takers and Prudential Regulation Authority—supervisory approach—insurers for more information on the PRA's approach to supervision.

tr:secmain.core:title: Monitoring costs of the PRA
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, Sch 1ZB, para 23National Audit Act 1983, s 6The PRA must send its accounts for audit by the National Audit Office, which will also be able to commence value for money reviews of the PRA on its own initiative.

tr:secmain.core:title: Responsibility for the Financial Services Compensation Scheme
tr:secmain.core:para: FSMA 2000, Part XVBoth the FCA and the PRA have responsibility for the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) and for making rules relating to compensation and fees. The PRA is responsible for rules relating to deposits and insurance policy protection, while the FCA is responsible for the remaining types of financial activity covered by the FSCS. The regulators must consult each other as appropriate when formulating rules relating to the scheme.
The memorandum of understanding between the FCA and the PRA sets out how coordination between the regulators in relation to the FSCS will operate in practice.
